#### **Key Takeaways**


- Most technology environments were built to solve legitimate operational challenges but were rarely designed around a complete view of the guest.


- The hidden cost of disconnected technology is often an incomplete understanding of the guest, making it harder to recognize preferences, strengthen loyalty, and deliver connected experiences.


- AI delivers greater value when it operates on top of a connected technology foundation that provides a more complete view of the guest relationship.


One of the things I’ve come to appreciate recently is that many of the guest visibility challenges operators face today trace back to past technology decisions that were made for entirely valid reasons.


Technology environments are rarely built from a blank slate. They evolve over time as new operational requirements emerge, guest expectations change, and organizations look for ways to modernize different parts of the business. Hotel, food and beverage, loyalty, and gaming teams each invest in systems designed to solve specific business challenges.


In many cases, those decisions delivered significant value. Over time, however, many resorts accumulated systems the same way they accumulated amenities, with each technology investment solving a specific operational challenge without fully anticipating how guest expectations and technology requirements would evolve.


Now organizations are asking those systems to work together in support of something they were never originally designed to provide: a complete understanding of the guest relationship.


#### **Good Decisions Can Create Unexpected Complexity**


Looking back, many fragmented technology environments are really the product of dozens of reasonable decisions made over time.Every department wants technology that helps it operate more effectively and support its business strategy. Viewed through that lens, technology decisions often make complete sense at the time they’re made; however, the complexity emerges gradually.


Part of the reason is that guest relationships themselves have become more complex. A guest may interact with gaming, hospitality, loyalty, dining, entertainment, retail, and other areas of the resort during a single visit. Supporting those interactions across a guest’s journey is often a collection of systems acquired over many years to address individual operational requirements rather than function as a unified ecosystem. Today, delivering on guest expectations increasingly depends on how well those technologies work together, even though they were often selected independently and for very different purposes.


As guest interactions have expanded across the resort, technology environments have been asked to support increasingly complex relationships between systems, departments, and guest touchpoints. Gaming operators possess more information than ever before, but many of the technology environments supporting that information were never designed with a unified guest strategy in mind.


Employees feel the effects of those limitations every day. Their time is spent searching for details, switching between systems, and piecing together information that already exists somewhere within the organization. From the guest’s perspective, these limitations often appear as repeated questions, overlooked preferences, inconsistent recognition, or experiences that feel disconnected from previous interactions.


Disconnected technology is often discussed as a systems problem, but its effects are typically felt elsewhere. The hidden cost of disconnected technology is often an incomplete understanding of the guest. When information remains difficult to connect across the resort, organizations miss opportunities to recognize preferences and build more informed and loyal guest relationships.


#### **Why AI Is Bringing Greater Attention to the Issue**


As operators explore the potential of AI, they’re also taking a fresh look at technology challenges that have existed for years. As guest expectations have evolved, connected information has shifted from a competitive advantage and “nice to have” to an operational necessity. Employees need better context to serve guests effectively, and guests increasingly expect experiences that reflect their relationship with the property.


AI can help identify patterns and relationships that would otherwise remain difficult to recognize. Its ability to do so, however, depends heavily on the information available to it and how effectively that information can move across the technology environment supporting the resort. Technology environments built around isolated systems naturally limit what AI can see, while connected ecosystems make it easier to surface context across the different departments of the operation. As a result, organizations are increasingly recognizing that AI success is influenced as much by the connectedness of their technology ecosystem as the capabilities of the AI itself.


#### **Technology Foundations Matter More Than Ever**


For years, technology decisions were often evaluated based on the operational challenges they helped solve. Did the system improve efficiency? Did it support the needs of a specific department? Did it deliver measurable value for the team using it?


Those questions still matter, but what has changed is the increasing importance of understanding how technology contributes to the broader guest relationship. As operators pursue AI, personalization, loyalty, and guest intelligence initiatives, they’re discovering that the ability to connect information across the resort is becoming just as important as the capabilities of any individual application.


A dining preference captured during one interaction can influence future loyalty engagement. A hotel stay can provide context around gaming behavior. Entertainment attendance may reveal long-term guest value that would never be apparent through gaming activity alone. The more easily information can move across the organization, the more opportunities operators have to recognize those connections.


AI tends to deliver the greatest value when it’s supported by technology environments that make it easier for guest information to move across the resort. Operational data has never been more abundant, but its value ultimately depends on an organization’s ability to bring that information together in ways that benefit employees and guests.


#### **Looking Beyond Systems**


The gaming industry has spent decades refining its understanding of player behavior, but what continues to evolve is the industry’s ability to extend that same understanding across the broader guest relationship. The hidden cost of disconnected technology extends far beyond fragmented information. It affects a guest journey that increasingly spans gaming, hospitality, dining, entertainment, loyalty, and every other interaction with the property. Guests don’t separate those experiences into departments, and they don’t distinguish between hotel systems, loyalty systems, restaurant systems, or gaming systems. They simply experience a visit.


And that raises an important question: if guests experience the resort as a single journey, why are so many of the technologies supporting that journey still operating independently? That’s the topic I’ll explore in the next article.
